quickAnswer: The Frame Rate Judder & Pacing Test benchmarks your monitor or television for motion smoothness, display cadence dividers, and sample-and-hold OLED stutter. It features an interactive quad-cadence raster motion sweep comparing 30 FPS, 40 FPS, 60 FPS, and native display refresh rates in real time, a high-precision browser refresh rate detector, and a display cadence calculator illustrating why 40 FPS modes require a 120Hz container ($120 / 40 = 3$). All telemetry executes locally in browser memory.

howTo.name: Connect Your Gaming Display
howTo.text: Open this diagnostic on your PC, laptop, or console browser connected to your gaming monitor or television.

howTo.name: Observe Quad-Cadence Motion Bars
howTo.text: Track the moving raster bars with your eyes. Compare the perceived stepping and jitter between 30 FPS, 40 FPS, 60 FPS, and native display refresh.

howTo.name: Check Hardware Telemetry
howTo.text: Inspect the live FPS and frame-time delta metrics to verify whether your operating system and browser deliver true 60Hz or 120Hz pacing.

howTo.name: Calculate Display Cadence Dividers
howTo.text: Select your game target frame rate and display refresh rate in the cadence calculator to see if the frame times divide evenly or induce pulldown judder.

howTo.name: Evaluate VRR and LFC Boundaries
howTo.text: Toggle the VRR option to inspect whether your target framerate falls inside the native 48Hz-120Hz window or triggers Low Framerate Compensation.

faq.q: Why does 30 FPS look choppy on OLED televisions compared to older LCDs?
faq.a: OLED pixels possess near-instantaneous response times (under 0.1 ms GtG), whereas older LCD panels exhibited 5 to 15 ms of liquid crystal transition blur. On sample-and-hold OLED displays, each 30 FPS frame remains completely static for 33.3 milliseconds before instantly stepping to the next position. Because your retina tracks continuous motion across the screen, this instant stepping creates high-contrast retinal judder. The older LCD panel's slow response time created natural motion blur that masked this stepping [Confirmed: Blur Busters, DisplayMate].

faq.q: Why do 40 FPS console modes require a 120Hz display?
faq.a: On a standard 60Hz display, 40 FPS does not divide evenly: 60 divided by 40 equals 1.5 display refreshes per frame. The television must alternate between holding a frame for 1 refresh (16.67 ms) and 2 refreshes (33.33 ms), creating severe rhythmic 3:2 judder. On a 120Hz display, 120 divided by 40 equals exactly 3.0 refreshes per frame. Every frame is displayed for precisely 25.0 milliseconds in an even 1:1:1 integer cadence, eliminating judder while saving ~33% GPU render budget compared to 60 FPS [Confirmed: Sony Interactive Entertainment, Digital Foundry].

faq.q: What is the HDMI 2.1 VRR 48Hz floor and what is LFC?
faq.a: Standard HDMI 2.1 Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) modules operate within a hardware frequency window of 48 Hz to 120 Hz. When a game's frame rate drops below 48 FPS (such as a 30 FPS title), the display cannot match the frame rate 1:1. The console and display engage Low Framerate Compensation (LFC), which multiplies frames (e.g. duplicating 30 FPS frames twice to refresh at 60 Hz). On OLED televisions, rapid transitions across the 48Hz boundary can cause slight gamma luminance shifts perceived as near-black flicker.

faq.q: Can a web browser diagnose what a PS5 or Xbox outputs directly over HDMI?
faq.a: No. A web browser running on a PC, Mac, or smartphone cannot intercept raw HDMI video signals output from an external console. This diagnostic benchmarks the physical panel's local motion cadence, display refresh synchronization, and browser rendering pipeline to verify your screen's motion reproduction characteristics.

faq.q: Why does my 120Hz or 144Hz screen report 60Hz in this browser test?
faq.a: Common causes include: (1) Operating system display settings defaulted to 60Hz; (2) The connected HDMI or DisplayPort cable does not meet High Speed or Ultra High Speed bandwidth specifications; (3) Browser hardware acceleration is disabled; (4) On Apple Safari for iOS, the 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps' feature flag is active by default in Settings.

articleHtml:
Display Motion Cadence, Sample-and-Hold OLED Stutter, and the 40 FPS Paradigm

As console hardware transitions into advanced 9th-generation visual features, understanding the intersection of display refresh rates, frame pacing cadences, and panel response characteristics is essential for both competitive and cinematic gameplay.

Sample-and-Hold Displays and Retinal Stutter

Almost all modern consumer displays—including OLED, QD-OLED, and LCD panels—operate on the sample-and-hold principle. Unlike legacy cathode-ray tube (CRT) displays or plasma televisions that flashed phosphor light for fractions of a millisecond and decayed to black before the next scan, sample-and-hold panels display a static frame continuously until the pixel elements are refreshed with the next frame's data.

When a human eye tracks a moving object across the screen, the eye moves smoothly. However, the object on screen remains stationary for the entire frame hold duration (33.3 milliseconds at 30 FPS). Because the image is frozen while the eye is continuously moving, the image is smeared across the retina. On older LCD panels, liquid crystal molecules took 5 to 15 milliseconds to shift color (Grey-to-Grey transition), producing natural motion blur that softened the transition between frames. Modern OLED displays, by contrast, feature instantaneous pixel response times under 0.1 milliseconds. With zero transition blur, the 33.3 millisecond static hold creates severe, jarring retinal stepping perceived as motion judder or stutter during camera panning.

The Mathematics of 40 FPS: Why $120 / 40 = 3$ is the Golden Cadence

For decades, console developers faced a binary compromise: locked 30 FPS (high visual fidelity, dense ray tracing, but choppy motion) or locked 60 FPS (fluid motion, but requiring severe compromises to rendering resolution, asset density, and geometry). With the widespread adoption of HDMI 2.1 televisions supporting native 120Hz refresh rates, a third option emerged: the 40 FPS balanced fidelity mode [Confirmed: Sony Interactive Entertainment, Insomniac Games].

The elegance of 40 FPS is grounded in integer cadence dividers:

$$\text{Refreshes per Frame (60Hz)} = \frac{60\text{ Hz}}{40\text{ FPS}} = 1.5\text{ (Asymmetric 1:2 repeat - Severe Judder)}$$
$$\text{Refreshes per Frame (120Hz)} = \frac{120\text{ Hz}}{40\text{ FPS}} = 3.0\text{ (Uniform 1:1:1 integer cadence - Flawless)}$$

On a 60Hz display, a 40 FPS feed must alternate between being shown for 1 display refresh (16.67 ms) and 2 display refreshes (33.33 ms), creating unbearable rhythmic judder. On a 120Hz display, however, 120 divides cleanly by 40 into exactly 3 refreshes per frame. Every game frame is scanned for precisely 25.0 milliseconds. This reduces frame hold time by 25% compared to 30 FPS (from 33.3 ms down to 25.0 ms), eliminating retinal stutter while requiring only a 33% increase in rendering workload over 30 FPS, compared to the 100% rendering increase required for locked 60 FPS.

HDMI 2.1 VRR Hardware Floor and Low Framerate Compensation

Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) allows the display panel to synchronize its refresh timing directly with the GPU's frame presentation, eliminating tearing and stuttering when frame rates fluctuate. However, physical display timing controllers (TCONs) possess physical minimum operating thresholds. In HDMI 2.1 and VESA Adaptive-Sync standards, the native VRR window typically operates from 48 Hz to 120 Hz.

When a console title runs below 48 FPS (such as a 30 FPS or 40 FPS mode), the display cannot cycle at 30 Hz without panel flicker or voltage decay. To overcome this, the graphics hardware initiates Low Framerate Compensation (LFC). LFC multiplies each frame—for example, presenting a 30 FPS frame twice so the panel operates at 60 Hz, or presenting a 40 FPS frame twice to run at 80 Hz.

While LFC preserves smooth motion, users on OLED panels may observe subtle gamma flickering in dark game environments. Because OLED pixel luminance curves vary slightly across different refresh frequencies, rapid shifts between native VRR frequencies and multiplied LFC frequencies cause minute voltage fluctuations in dark gray tones, producing visible near-black flicker.

Step-by-Step Console and Display Calibration Checklist

  1. Verify HDMI Port Bandwidth: Ensure your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X is connected to an HDMI 2.1 port rated for 40 Gbps or 48 Gbps (often labeled HDMI 3 or HDMI 4 / eARC on LG and Sony televisions).
  2. Enable Enhanced HDMI Signal: In television picture settings, set the HDMI input format to 'Enhanced Format (VRR)' on Sony, 'HDMI Ultra HD Deep Color' on LG, or 'Game Mode' on Samsung.
  3. Activate 120Hz Output in Console Settings: On PS5, navigate to Settings > Screen and Video > 120 Hz Output and set to 'Automatic'. On Xbox Series X, navigate to TV & Display Options > Resolution: 4K UHD and Refresh Rate: 120 Hz.
  4. Calibrate HGiG Tone Mapping: In your television picture settings under Tone Mapping, select HGiG (HDR Gaming Interest Group) rather than dynamic tone mapping (DTM) before running the console's HDR calibration wizard. This prevents double-tonemapping and preserves specular highlight detail up to the panel's clipping point.
  5. Disable Motion Smoothing: Turn off motion interpolation (TruMotion, Motionflow, Auto Motion Plus) in Game Mode to avoid introducing 50 to 80 milliseconds of input latency.
